subject: Anatomy
summary: The placenta is a temporary organ that connects the developing fetus to the uterine wall. It facilitates nutrient uptake, waste elimination, and gas exchange via the mother's blood supply. It also produces hormones essential for pregnancy maintenance.

sections.p: The placenta is a vital, transient organ that develops during pregnancy. It serves as the interface between the mother and the fetus, enabling the exchange of gases, nutrients, and waste products. It also plays a crucial endocrine role.
b: Forms early in pregnancy.
Expelled after the fetus is born.
Essential for fetal survival and growth.
Implantation site is usually fundal or high lateral.
Fetal surface is smooth and shiny.
Maternal surface is rough and lobulated.

sections.p: The placenta is intimately related to the decidua basalis of the uterine wall, forming the maternal side. The fetal side is covered by the amnion and chorion, which also form the umbilical cord. The amniotic fluid surrounds the fetus and the fetal surface of the placenta.
b: Connected to fetus via umbilical cord.
Adheres to the uterine lining (decidua).
Surrounded by amniotic fluid.

sections.p: The placenta receives maternal blood from the uterine arteries and returns it via the uterine veins. Fetal blood circulates within the placental villi, supplied by the umbilical arteries and drained by the umbilical vein. This dual circulation allows for efficient exchange.
b: Maternal: Uterine arteries and veins.
Fetal: Umbilical arteries and vein.
Exchange occurs across villous membrane.

sections.p: The placenta itself lacks intrinsic nerve supply. Its functions are regulated by maternal and fetal hormonal and vascular mechanisms. Autonomic nerves in the uterine wall influence blood flow to the placenta.
b: No direct innervation.
Regulation is hormonal and vascular.
Uterine nerves affect placental blood flow.

sections.p: The placenta performs several critical functions: gas exchange (oxygen and carbon dioxide), nutrient transfer (glucose, amino acids, fats, vitamins, minerals), waste removal (urea, bilirubin), antibody transfer (passive immunity), and hormone production (progesterone, estrogen, hCG) to maintain pregnancy.
b: Respiration: O2 in, CO2 out.
Nutrition: Supplies nutrients to fetus.
Excretion: Removes fetal waste.
Endocrine: Produces pregnancy hormones.
Immunological: Transfers maternal antibodies.

sections.p: Abnormalities in placental location or function can lead to significant complications. Placenta previa, where the placenta covers the cervix, necessitates Cesarean delivery. Placental abruption, the premature separation from the uterine wall, causes maternal hemorrhage and fetal distress. Poor placental function can result in fetal growth restriction.
b: Placenta previa: covers cervix.
Placental abruption: premature separation.
Placental insufficiency: poor fetal growth.

sections.p: When examining the placenta after delivery, note its size, shape, and completeness. Ensure no fragments are retained in the uterus, which can cause postpartum hemorrhage or infection. The umbilical cord should have three vessels (two arteries, one vein).
b: Check for completeness.
Inspect umbilical cord vessels.
Assess for abnormalities.

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of fetal distress (decreased fetal movements).

faq.q: What is the main role of the placenta?
faq.a: To provide oxygen and nutrients to the fetus and remove waste products.
A condition where the placenta partially or completely covers the cervix, often leading to bleeding.

faq.q: Can the placenta cause problems after birth?
faq.a: Yes, retained placental fragments can cause bleeding or infection.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: Focused obstetric history and a systematic placental examination identify abnormal implantation, bleeding risk and retained tissue.
b: Gestational age and dating method
Onset, amount and character of vaginal bleeding
Pain presence or absence and uterine tenderness
Previous cesarean sections or uterine surgery
History of placenta previa or accreta in prior pregnancies
Maternal hypertension, diabetes, HIV or anemia
Use of anticoagulants, herbal medicines or tobacco

t.a: Inspection of the perineum and vagina
t.b: Detect active bleeding or clots; a bright red, painless flow suggests previa, while painful bleeding suggests abruption. Cannot determine depth of placental attachment.

t.a: Palpation of the uterus (fundal height, tenderness)
t.b: Assess uterine size for gestational age and detect uterine rigidity (abruption). Palpation cannot locate the placental edge.
Identify fetal distress secondary to placental insufficiency. Does not quantify placental location.

t.a: Assessment of placenta after delivery (visual inspection, cord length, membranes)
t.b: Look for completeness, lobulation, retro‑placental clots, and cord insertion. Cannot diagnose previa or accreta retrospectively.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Imaging and laboratory tests confirm placental position, assess fetal well‑being and detect maternal complications.

t.b: Answers: placental location and type (previa, low‑lying, accreta). A placenta covering the internal os = complete previa. Low‑lying = edge <2 cm from os. If unavailable, rely on clinical suspicion and refer.
Answers: precise distance of placental edge from cervical os. Distance ≥2 cm = safe for vaginal delivery; <2 cm = increased bleeding risk, plan cesarean. If not available, manage as previa.

Answers: severity of blood loss. Hemoglobin <8 g/dL or hematocrit <24 % signals need for transfusion. If labs unavailable, assess clinical shock signs.

Answers: depth of placental invasion into myometrium. Loss of placental-myometrial interface indicates accreta. If MRI unavailable, plan for surgical preparedness and possible hysterectomy.

sections.p: Classification systems guide management and referral decisions for placental disorders.
b: Placenta previa: complete (covers os), partial (covers part), marginal (edge ≤2 cm), low‑lying (edge >2 cm but <5 cm).
Placental accreta spectrum: accreta (adherent), increta (invasion into myometrium), percreta (through uterine serosa).
Placental abruption grading: Grade I (mild, concealed), Grade II (moderate, painful bleeding), Grade III (severe, hemodynamic instability).

sections.p: Differential diagnoses that mimic placental pathology must be considered, especially in low‑resource settings.

t.a: Uterine fibroids protruding into lower segment
t.b: May cause painless bleeding and low‑lying mass on exam. Ultrasound shows hypoechoic solid lesions distinct from placental tissue.
Produce fresh vaginal bleeding but are visualized on speculum exam; ultrasound shows normal placental location.
Painless bleeding with fetal heart rate decelerations; transvaginal color Doppler shows vessels crossing os, not placental tissue.
Severe pain, loss of fetal station, abnormal fetal heart pattern; clinical exam reveals uterine defect, not placental previa.

sections.p: Immediate stabilization, definitive treatment, monitoring, escalation and referral for placenta previa or accreta.
b: 1. Assess airway, breathing, circulation; stop bleeding with uterine massage and uterine tamponade if needed.
2. Confirm diagnosis with ultrasound; if placenta covers os, plan for elective Caesarean at 36–37 weeks.
3. Administer antenatal corticosteroids if <34 weeks to mature fetal lungs.
4. Give prophylactic broad‑spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin + gentamicin) to reduce infection risk.
5. Administer uterotonics (oxytocin infusion) after delivery to prevent hemorrhage.
6. If bleeding persists, give tranexamic acid to reduce fibrinolysis; avoid if active thromboembolism suspected.
7. Monitor maternal vitals, hemoglobin, urine output hourly; check for signs of shock.
8. Escalate to higher‑level facility if massive transfusion required, uncontrolled bleeding, or signs of organ failure.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Key adverse effects of uterotonics and antifibrinolytics and how to manage them.
b: Oxytocin: tachycardia, hypotension, water intoxication; treat with fluid restriction and slow infusion.
Tranexamic acid: nausea, vomiting, rare seizures; monitor for seizures and discontinue if severe.
Antibiotics: allergic rash, nephrotoxicity (gentamicin); monitor renal function and stop if creatinine rises.
Antifibrinolytics can increase thrombus risk; avoid in patients with recent thromboembolism or clotting disorders.

sections.p: Recognise life‑threatening events and thresholds for referral.
b: 2. Hypotension <90 mmHg systolic or MAP <65 mmHg: start IV fluids and consider blood transfusion.
3. Oliguria <30 mL/h or anuria: suspect renal failure, refer for ICU care.
4. Signs of DIC (prolonged PT/PTT, low fibrinogen, thrombocytopenia): start plasma and cryoprecipitate, refer for specialist care.
5. Fetal distress on cardiotocography: prepare for emergency Caesarean.

sections.p: How comorbidities alter presentation, investigations and treatment.
b: HIV: increased risk of infection; use WHO‑recommended prophylaxis and monitor CD4 counts.
TB: may cause anemia and malnutrition; adjust antibiotic regimens to avoid hepatotoxicity.
Malnutrition: low albumin can mask bleeding; use albumin infusion cautiously.
Diabetes: higher risk of infection and impaired wound healing; control glucose tightly.
Herbal remedies: some (e.g., kava) can potentiate bleeding; ask about use.
Alcohol: liver dysfunction may affect drug metabolism; avoid hepatotoxic drugs.
Renal failure: avoid nephrotoxic antibiotics; monitor drug levels.
Liver failure: avoid hepatotoxic drugs; use low‑dose tranexamic acid cautiously.
Age extremes: elderly may have reduced physiologic reserve; children require weight‑adjusted doses.

sections.p: Tailored care for vulnerable populations in low‑resource settings.
b: Children: rare but possible placental disorders; use paediatric dosing and monitor for growth restriction.
Pregnancy: all interventions must consider fetal safety; avoid teratogenic drugs.
Elderly: higher bleeding risk; monitor vitals closely and use lower drug doses.
People with HIV: ensure ART is continued; avoid drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
Low‑resource settings: use WHO‑recommended oxytocin and tranexamic acid; rely on clinical assessment when labs unavailable; refer when transfusion or ICU needed.

facts: Placenta previa is classified as major when the placenta covers the internal os and minor when it is within 2 cm of the os.
The normal thickness of the placenta at term is 2–4 cm; >5 cm suggests placental edema or infarction.
Umbilical artery Doppler pulsatility index >95th percentile indicates fetal compromise.
Placental abruption risk increases with hypertension, trauma, and cocaine use; incidence ~1% of pregnancies.
Maternal blood flow to the placenta is supplied by uterine arteries arising from internal iliac arteries.
Fetal blood enters the placenta via two umbilical arteries and returns via one umbilical vein.
Placental insufficiency is diagnosed when fetal growth restriction <10th percentile with abnormal Doppler studies.
The placenta is expelled within 30 minutes of fetal delivery in >95% of normal labours.

vivas.q: Define placenta previa and differentiate major from minor types.
vivas.a: Placenta previa is implantation of placental tissue over the cervical os; major covers the os, minor lies within 2 cm of it but does not cover it.

vivas.q: What is the immediate management of a 30‑year‑old at 32 weeks with painless bleeding and complete placenta previa?
vivas.a: Stabilise, give IV fluids, give corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity, admit for observation, and plan elective Caesarean at 36‑37 weeks; avoid digital vaginal exam.

vivas.q: How would you manage a 26‑year‑old at 24 weeks with painless bleeding and placenta previa?
vivas.a: Hospitalise, give fluids, give corticosteroids, monitor fetal wellbeing, counsel pelvic rest, and plan delivery by Caesarean at 36‑37 weeks; no labour induction.

vivas.q: Which blastocyst structure forms the fetal component of the placenta?
vivas.a: The chorionic villi derived from the trophoblast of the blastocyst.

vivas.q: State a true physiological capability of the human placenta.
vivas.a: It can transfer maternal IgG antibodies to the fetus, providing passive immunity.

vivas.q: What term describes a genetic abnormality confined to placental tissue?
A facility performs manual removal of placenta, gives oxytocin and magnesium sulphate. What level of emergency obstetric care is this?
vivas.a: It provides comprehensive emergency obstetric care (CEmOC) as it can manage postpartum haemorrhage and eclampsia.

vivas.q: What classic sign indicates placental separation during the third stage?
vivas.a: A gush of blood followed by a well‑defined, rounded, firm placenta and the lengthening of the umbilical cord.

vivas.q: After active management of the third stage, how often should the mother be observed in the first hour?
vivas.a: Every 15 minutes for the first hour to detect early postpartum haemorrhage.

vivas.q: Explain why digital vaginal examination is avoided in suspected placenta previa.
vivas.a: It can disrupt the placental attachment, causing severe bleeding and maternal/fetal compromise.

vivas.q: How do you differentiate placenta previa from abruptio placentae on ultrasound?
vivas.a: Previa shows low‑lying placental tissue over the os; abruptio shows retroplacental clot and a normal placental location.

vivas.q: What bedside test can assess placental separation after delivery?
vivas.a: The ‘uterine fundal height’ drops by 2‑3 cm and the uterus becomes firm; palpation of the uterine edge confirms separation.

vivas.q: When is a Caesarean section indicated for placenta previa?
vivas.a: When the placenta is major previa, or any previa with active bleeding, or when labour begins.

vivas.q: Why is magnesium sulphate given in severe pre‑eclampsia with placenta previa?
vivas.a: To prevent seizures; it does not affect placental location but controls maternal neurologic complications.

vivas.q: What are the key maternal cardiovascular adaptations in pregnancy that affect placental perfusion?
vivas.a: Blood volume ↑ ≈ 40%, cardiac output ↑ ≈ 30‑50%, systemic vascular resistance ↓, uterine artery flow ↑; these maintain placental exchange.

vivas.q: List three common placental abnormalities and their clinical significance.
vivas.a: Placenta previa (bleeding, preterm delivery), abruptio placentae (painful bleeding, fetal distress), velamentous insertion (vessel rupture, fetal loss).

vivas.q: What is the role of corticosteroids in placenta previa management?
vivas.a: To accelerate fetal lung maturity when delivery is anticipated before 34 weeks.

vivas.q: How does HIV infection alter placental function?
vivas.a: It may increase risk of placental insufficiency and vertical transmission; antiretroviral therapy reduces these risks.

mcqs.q: A 28‑year‑old at 35 weeks presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a low‑lying placenta 1 cm from the internal os. The best next step is:
mcqs.e: A low‑lying placenta without active bleeding is managed expectantly; delivery is planned by Caesarean at 36‑37 weeks.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of placental abruption?
mcqs.e: Placental abruption usually presents with painful bleeding; painless bleeding suggests previa.

mcqs.q: The fetal side of the placenta is characterized by:
mcqs.e: The fetal surface is smooth and shiny, covered by the amnion.

mcqs.q: Which drug is given to prevent seizures in a woman with severe pre‑eclampsia and placenta previa?
mcqs.e: Magnesium sulphate is the anticonvulsant of choice in severe pre‑eclampsia.

mcqs.q: In a low‑resource setting without Doppler, which clinical sign suggests fetal compromise due to placental insufficiency?
mcqs.e: Reduced fetal movements are an early bedside indicator of fetal compromise.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes confined placental mosaicism?
o: Genetic abnormality present only in fetal cells
Chromosomal abnormality limited to placental tissue
mcqs.e: It refers to a chromosomal abnormality that is present only in placental cells, not the fetus.

cases.v: A 32‑year‑old G2P1 at 33 weeks gestation presents with sudden painless vaginal bleeding. No uterine tenderness. Ultrasound shows the placenta covering the internal os.

qs.q: What is the most appropriate immediate management?
qs.a: Stabilise, give IV fluids, administer corticosteroids, admit for observation, and plan elective Caesarean at 36‑37 weeks; avoid vaginal examination.

qs.q: Which sign would you look for to assess severity of bleeding?
qs.a: Maternal vital signs (BP, pulse), haemoglobin level, and amount of blood loss; a drop in haemoglobin >2 g/dL indicates significant bleed.

qs.q: When can a trial of labour be considered in placenta previa?
qs.a: Only if the placenta has migrated >2 cm away from the os on repeat ultrasound after 36 weeks and there is no active bleeding.

cases.v: A 24‑year‑old primigravida at 24 weeks presents with painless vaginal bleeding. Ultrasound shows a low‑lying placenta 1.5 cm from the internal os, no fetal distress.

qs.a: Hospitalise, give IV fluids, give corticosteroids for lung maturity, advise pelvic rest, monitor haemoglobin and fetal heart rate, repeat ultrasound at 28 weeks.

qs.q: What bedside observation is essential during the first hour after admission?
qs.a: Check maternal vitals and bleeding every 15 minutes; assess fetal heart rate twice hourly.

qs.q: Which investigation is most useful if Doppler is unavailable?
qs.a: Serial fundal height measurements and maternal symptom review; a sudden slowdown in growth suggests placental insufficiency.

mistakes: Performing a digital vaginal exam in suspected placenta previa, leading to severe hemorrhage.
Confusing placenta previa with abruptio placentae; missing uterine tenderness and painful bleeding.
Failing to give corticosteroids before planned early delivery, increasing neonatal respiratory risk.
Assuming all low‑lying placentas require Caesarean; many migrate upward and can be delivered vaginally.
Not monitoring maternal vitals every 15 minutes in the first hour, missing early postpartum haemorrhage.
Neglecting to assess fetal movements as a bedside indicator of placental insufficiency in low‑resource settings.
Using ergometrine in a woman with hypertension or pre‑eclampsia, risking severe hypertension.
Overlooking confined placental mosaicism and misinterpreting CVS results as fetal abnormality.
